title: Spain's migrant surge reignites debate over Europe’s Islamist terror threat
summary: Spain recorded the EU's highest number of jihadist terrorism arrests in 2025 as suspected extremists were identified among 72,000 migrants flooding into Ceuta.
story: Lorenzo Vidino warns the Senate about the Muslim Brotherhood's covert influence inside the United States. He explains how the group infiltrates American education and politics to advance its agenda.

The estimated 72,000 Moroccan migrants who flooded into the Spanish city of Ceuta within 24 hours is shining a spotlight on Europe’s massive problem of illegal and legal migration and the threat of growing Islamic terrorism.
Mideast and European commentators who closely follow Islamic extremism across the continent say Europe’s political class needs to tackle the origins of radical Islamism to prevent terrorism.

According to a July Europol (formerly known as the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation) report, Spain recorded the highest number of arrests (117) for "jihadist terrorism-related offenses" within the European Union during 2025.
CEUTA MIGRANT SURGE EXPOSES SPAIN-MOROCCO TENSIONS AS ISLAMIST GROUPS REPORTEDLY SEEK TO EXPLOIT BORDER CRISIS

Moroccan security forces clash with migrants attempting to cross into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta near the town of Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border July 31, 2026. (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images)

Some Spanish outlets claimed the Spanish Civil Guard and police identified "about a dozen" individuals previously deported from Spain for suspected terror-related offenses among those who entered Ceuta last week. However, Euro News reported that Spain’s interior ministry said it has not confirmed those reports.

Quoting the ministry, it reported, "The Spanish public and the people of Ceuta can be confident that the arrivals on 30 July do not pose a threat to public security." The report also cited the interior ministry as saying that, so far this year, 82 people had been arrested for offenses related to jihadist terrorism.

Lorenzo Vidino, director of the Program on Extremism at The George Washington University and an expert on Islamism in Europe and North America, told Fox News Digital, "This is Europe. This is the way it has been for the last 15 years, with some ebbs and flows.
"It is more in line with the last 10 years. Europe has sadly learned to live with this reality," he added of the new Europol report.

British political commentator and Mideast expert Tom Gross told Fox News Digital, "Europe’s ruling classes need to be honest. It is not racist to point out the obvious: that most terrorism in Western Europe today is being fueled by radical Islamic mosques and teachers.
GERMAN OFFICIALS WANT TO KNOW WHY BERLIN ATTACK SUSPECT WAS FREE DESPITE ALLEGED ISIS SUPPORT
Police officers stand near a vehicle that crashed into a tree after traveling into a crowd near Berlin's annual Pride event in Berlin, Germany, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)
"Leaders in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Egypt acknowledge this. Why can’t Western leaders?"

Gross said, "Politicians such as new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, London Mayor Sadiq Khan and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez need to stop fueling the propaganda of radical Muslims by implying that there has been some kind of genocide against Muslims in Gaza, when there has been nothing of the sort.

"If they really want to help push back radical Islam, European leaders should be assisting, not criticizing, those in Washington and elsewhere calling for the downfall of Iran’s Islamic dictatorship."

In April, the U.K. raised its national terror threat level to "severe" after an antisemitic attack in London when a Somali immigrant stabbed two men. A "severe" warning, according to authorities, means another terrorist attack is considered "highly likely" in the next six months.

A spokesperson for London’s Mayor Khan told Fox News Digital. "The Mayor has invested £16 million (approxmiately $21.5 million) — more than any other mayor — to support grassroots community groups to stand up to hate and intolerance. This includes £6 million (approximately $8 million) through his Shared Endeavour Fund to give Londoners the tools and skills to tackle extremism."
GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS
Law enforcement patrol immediately after a stabbing attack in Paris July 27, 2026. (Kenzo Tribouillard/Getty Images)

Late last month, an alleged Islamist State terrorist, 21-year-old German-Lebanese man Abdul Ballout, allegedly drove a van into the Berlin Pride Parade event, murdering one woman and injuring nearly 30 people. The German authorities had released Ballout despite his recent conviction related to supporting the Islamic State.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told public broadcaster ZDF during an interview that, in light of the 21-year-old suspect's conviction and record of backing the Islamic State, it did not make sense that the man was roaming free.
"You can assume that it certainly would have made sense to put this person in custody," he noted.

Khan’s spokesperson also cited an X post from the mayor after the Berlin Pride attack: "My thoughts are with everyone affected by the horrific attack in Berlin and their families. This appalling act of violence has no place in our society. London stands in solidarity with Berlin’s LGBTQ+ community. This is why Pride matters. Those who seek to spread hatred and division will never win."
SCATHING REPORT CALLS ON US TO LABEL ISLAMIST GROUP INFILTRATING ALL ASPECTS OF AMERICAN LIFE AS TERRORIST ORG

Firefighters tackle a blaze at Highfield Road in the Golders Green neighborhood of London after an arson attack on four charity ambulances belonging to the Jewish Community volunteer Ambulance Service. (PA/PA Images via Getty Images)

A new report by Germany’s federal intelligence that documents threats to the constitutional order estimates there are roughly 28,000 members in Germany’s Islamist scene. Approximately 9,110 are assessed to have an "orientation to violence.
"The type of violence is defined as jihadi violence," the report states.

Germany’s federal interior ministry, which publishes the annual domestic intelligence threat report, notes that crimes attributed to "religious ideology" have climbed from 134 in 2022 to 998 last year. Radical Islamist crimes are reportedly understood to make up the main portion of the "religious ideology" category.

Germany’s neighbor, France, experienced another stabbing just days after the attack in Germany. A suspect reportedly stabbed three women in Paris and, as people captured him after the attack, declared, "It is Allah who commanded me."

"The incident in Paris, it seems, (is) one of the cases" regarding how an attack is classified: ‘Is it terrorism? Is it a crazy guy?’" Vidino said. "Often times, Europeans play down the ideological motive and cite mental health. Some countries tend to do it more than others. Most Europeans go for downplaying of the ideological component."
AMERICAN ‘JIHAD’ FUELED BY 'RISKY SOURCE' INSIDE US BORDERS, WARNS NATIONAL SECURITY EXPERT

Austria’s intelligence agency announced in May on its website that it had arrested a group of suspected Islamist terrorists, which included five males between the ages of 14 and 45 and one 16-year-old female.

"The individuals concerned are suspected of having committed offenses related to Islamist extremism and terrorism in Austria, for example through membership of a terrorist organization, incitement to terrorist offenses, dissemination of IS [Islamic State] propaganda, and approval of terrorist offenses," the Austrian agency wrote.

In June, Swedish authorities arrested a teenage boy who pledged allegiance to the Islamist State and idolized suicide bombers, according to Swedish media. He allegedly issued death threats to students at school and showed pictures of beheaded people.

Nervana Mahmoud, a British Egyptian medical doctor who has written extensively about Islamist terrorism and indoctrination, told Fox News Digital, "The current challenge facing Europe is, in many ways, a battle over Islamist extremism and its place within Western societies. To address the threat at its source, European governments need to focus on preventing radicalization and disrupting foreign funding and ideological networks that fuel extremist movements. Without tackling these root causes, the risk of future terrorist attacks will remain."
SENATE CLEARS WAY FOR TRUMP'S TOP SPY AS KEY ANTI-TERROR PROGRAM REMAINS IN LIMBO
A map depicting Spain, Morocco and Spain's Cueta, which borders Morocco. (2026 EarthStar Geographics, OpenMapTiles, OpenStreetMap contributors)

The United Kingdom’s judicial system recorded a series of convictions of Islamist terrorists in July. Late last month, in Wigston, Britain, the authorities arrested a 27-year-old man for supporting the Islamic State.

A spokesperson for the British Home Office told Fox News Digital, "The United Kingdom has one of the most robust counterterrorism systems in the world. UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC
Prime Minister Keir Starmer visits the Hatzola Northwest independent ambulance base after a terrorist incident April 30, 2026, in Golders Green, England. (James Smith/Sam Snap/Getty Images)

Northern continental Europe is also facing a serious Jihadi terrorist threat. According to a late May Danish Security and Intelligence Service statement, the "CTA [Center for Terror Analysis in Denmark] assesses that the terrorist threat from militant Islamists remains at the level of significant."

title: Trump ally 'El Tigre' sworn in as Colombia's new president amid continent's rightward shift
summary: Abelardo de la Espriella inherits soaring violence, a fragmented Congress and a $34 billion financing gap as he vows to rebuild U.S. ties.
story: Abelardo de la Espriella, nicknamed 'The Tiger,' rallies supporters after advancing to a runoff as Colombia prepares for a decisive June 21 vote. (Anadolu via Reuters.)

Colombia entered a new political chapter as conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn into office Friday, pledging to reverse much of former President Gustavo Petro’s left-wing agenda and restore a tougher approach to security, economic policy and relations with the United States.

Known by his nickname "El Tigre" (the tiger), his inauguration marks one of the most significant political shifts in Latin America in recent years. After four years of socialist President Gustavo Petro’s "Total Peace" strategy, expanding coca cultivation and increasingly strained relations with Washington, de la Espriella now faces the challenge of translating campaign promises into governing reality.

He was joined at the inauguration by several conservative presidents from across the region, including Argentina's Javier Milei, Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa and Chile’s José Antonio Kast. Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche was there as part of the U.S. delegation. Spain's King Felipe VI and FIFA President Gianni Infantino were also in attendance, The Associated Press reported.
TRUMP SAYS COLOMBIA'S 'EL TIGRE' WILL BE A 'GREAT PRESIDENT' AS SOCIALIST OPPONENT LAUNCHES LEGAL CHALLENGE
Abelardo de la Espriella is sworn in as president of Colombia during the presidential inauguration at Arena USC Aug. 7, 2026, in Cali, Colombia.   (Gabriel Aponte/Getty Images)

"I have come to close a long chapter of national resignation and, together with the people, embark on the most profound transformation of our destiny," De La Espriella said, according to Reuters while speaking at the Pichincha Battalion military base in Cali.
"I send a firm message to the Colombian people: The time has come to restore order, authority, and freedom."
Reuters said one of his first acts as president was to join The Shield of the Americas, founded by President Donald Trump.

For the U.S., Colombia remains its closest security partner in South America, a key trading ally and one of the region’s largest recipients of U.S. security assistance. Hundreds of American companies operate in Colombia, while the country’s security conditions directly affect regional migration, organized crime and narcotics trafficking.

On foreign policy, the new president has committed to rebuilding strategic ties with the United States, restoring close cooperation with Israel and adopting a tougher stance toward the authoritarian governments of Venezuela, Cuba and Nicaragua.

Whether those commitments produce measurable improvements, however, will depend on resources that remain in short supply. Camilo Guzmán, executive director of Libertank, told Fox News Digital that the country’s financial situation will define what the administration can realistically accomplish.
Argentinian President Javier Milei arrives for the inauguration of Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella in Cali, Colombia, Friday, Aug. 7, 2026.  (Matias Delacroix/AP Photo)

"President de la Espriella inherits a house with the roof leaking and the safe empty. The order matters because almost everything he promised requires money he does not have." Guzmán pointed to Colombia’s deteriorating fiscal position as the administration’s most immediate challenge.

"Start with the fiscal picture. It is worse than his own team seems to expect. The 2026 deficit is tracking around 6.5-6.7% of GDP, the financing gap is close to $34 billion and the implicit medium-term adjustment being left on his desk is near five points of GDP. It is also a cash problem, not only an accounting one. Before he governs, he must make payroll."
WALTZ WARNS OF CHINESE, RUSSIAN-FUELED ‘NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT’ LOOMING CLOSE TO US SHORES

Colombia's right-wing presidential candidate, Abelardo de la Espriella, from the Defensores de la Patria movement, delivers a speech to supporters during a campaign rally in Palmira, near Cali, Colombia, May 14, 2026.  (Joaquin Sarmiento/AFP via Getty Images)

The International Monetary Fund projects Colombia’s economy will grow by only about 2.3% this year while inflation remains elevated, limiting the government’s room to finance new security initiatives or major economic reforms without additional spending cuts or new revenue measures.

Security presents an equally daunting challenge. Violence has intensified across several regions as criminal organizations and guerrilla groups have expanded their territorial influence over the past several years.

Guzmán said, "Security is the second fire. The first half of 2026 closed with the highest homicide count for any first semester in a decade, extortion still rising and armed groups that have grown sharply since 2022. Security is rebuilt in years, not in quarters. Expect operations, captures and hard rhetoric in the first 100 days, visible and real, but not yet structural."
Colombia's most wanted rebel leader appeals to ELN and other factions to form an insurgent bloc spanning Colombia and Venezuela. (Daniel Munoz/AFP via Getty Images)

Even if the administration moves quickly on executive actions, its legislative agenda will depend on building consensus in a fragmented Congress. Although De la Espriella won the presidency, his party controls only five seats in the Senate, while Petro’s Historic Pact remains the largest individual political bloc. Passing security reforms, fiscal legislation and broader economic initiatives will require negotiations with centrist and traditional parties on virtually every major proposal.

Guzmán believes those political realities may prove just as important as the security challenges. "He won the election; he did not win Congress. The July fight over the Senate presidency was the first warning. He has a coalition that is numerically large and poorly disciplined. His agenda will be negotiated bill by bill."
REPUBLICAN REP MARÍA ELVIRA SALAZAR DECLARES, 'AFTER CUBA, NICARAGUA IS NEXT'
Men work at a coca leaf field in Llorente, rural area of the port city of Tumaco, department of Narino, Colombia, Aug. 31, 2024. (Joaquin Sarmiento/AFP/Getty Images)

For that reason, analysts caution against measuring the administration’s success solely by immediate results. Instead, the first 100 days are likely to be judged by whether the new president establishes credibility, assembles an effective governing team and demonstrates that campaign promises can evolve into a coherent governing strategy.

Guzmán concluded, "The realistic expectation is this: the first 100 days will produce signals, not results. Appointments, decrees, an emergency spending cut, a tax bill, a security package. Meanwhile, expectations are enormous, and the distance between what people were promised and what is physically possible in 100 days is the main political risk he faces. He will spend those 100 days putting the house in order. He should say so out loud, and early. Credibility is the one asset he can build by day 100."
Colombian President Gustavo Petro delivers a speech during a troop recognition ceremony at the Jose Maria Cordova Military Cadet School in Bogota March 11, 2025. (Raul Arboleda/AFP via Getty Images)

The decisions investors and policymakers will watch most closely include whether De la Espriella formally abandons Petro’s negotiations with the ELN, resumes aerial coca fumigation, expands intelligence and security cooperation with Washington, restores full diplomatic engagement with Israel and introduces a credible fiscal adjustment plan.

Those early moves, analysts say, will offer the clearest indication of whether Colombia’s new president can begin delivering on his promise to reverse the Petro era, or whether the country’s fiscal, political and security realities will force him to scale back one of the most ambitious conservative agendas in modern Colombian politics.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.
Armando Regil Velasco reports on Mexico and Latin America. You can follow Armando on X @armando_regil

title: US intel warns Russia could launch limited attack on NATO ally in effort to fragment organization: report
summary: Vladimir Putin could attack a NATO member between this fall and 2029, U.S. intelligence assesses, likely targeting the Baltics or Poland directly.
story: Former CIA Station Chief Dan Hoffman discusses Russia's military struggles in Ukraine and concerns about expanding attacks in Europe. He highlighted Putin's threats and the importance of NATO unity and intelligence sharing.

Russian President Vladimir Putin could attack a NATO member country in the next few years in an attempt to fragment the post-World War II organization and test Article 5, new U.S. intelligence has found, according to a report.

While U.S. intelligence had previously assessed that Putin wouldn’t launch an assault on a NATO country while still involved in the war in Ukraine, the Russian president is now looking for a victory as Ukraine makes gains, and the U.S. and Europe have seen increasing signs he is testing the organization, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.
That includes a drone that hit a Romanian apartment building in May and cruise missiles that landed in Poland late last month, a NATO country.
RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS
Russian President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow Friday, Aug. 7, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)
Article 5 of NATO states that an attack on one country is an attack on all countries.
The assessment said it would likely be a limited attack that could range anywhere from a cyberattack to a small-scale land incursion and would likely be focused on the Baltics or Poland.
The attack could happen any time between this fall and 2029, the assessment said.

"The question mark is how the United States would respond in that case," Heather Conley, senior fellow with the American Enterprise Institute, told the Journal. "It has always been a goal [of Russia’s] to challenge the credibility of NATO and to separate the United States from its allies."
THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE
The assessment also comes amid claims the United States’ munitions stockpile has been depleted by arms sent to support Ukraine and due to the war in Iran.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, however, called those claims false.
Police and forensic investigators examine the location of impact after a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Galati, Romania, May 29, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

"We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing," Parnell told the Journal. "Across multiple combatant commands, we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests. Any adversary who confuses media noise with American weakness will discover the truth the hard way."
A land incursion was deemed the least likely because it would trigger Article 5, but it’s unclear what the response would be to something like a cyberattack.
REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

The Polish army secures a large crater, the probable impact site of a projectile linked to overnight strikes in Ukraine, in Tarnawa-Kolonia, eastern Poland, July 30, 2026. (TVN Poland/AFPTV/AFP via Getty Images)
"This has always been NATO’s challenge to respond to a sub-Article 5 attack, and it’s been very true that to this point, NATO allies have preferred not to escalate," Conley told the Journal.
Fox News Digital has reached out to NATO for comment.

Col. Martin O’Donnell, a NATO spokesman, told the Journal, "We are always thinking through and preparing for any number of scenarios. NATO is watching, and we are ready to deter and defend as necessary, which we continue to demonstrate."
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Student perpetrates deadly shooting at Thailand high school, authorities say
summary: A student opened fire at a high school in Thailand on Friday, ending the lives of at least six individuals and injuring others, police said.
story: Laura Ingraham, Jesse Watters and Sean Hannity bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

title: Kennedy Center board votes to add president’s name again — and throw in a ‘Trump Plaza’
summary: The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board on Thursday voted to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to one person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.
story: The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board on Thursday voted to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to one person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.

The decision would close the Kennedy Center’s main building while keeping a smaller addition, known as the Reach, open for some events in response to a May court order requiring the board to maintain the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.

After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20 to 3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change.
Trump, who appointed himself chairman of the board last year, joined the call for several minutes, according to the source who attended the meeting.
The three people voting against it were the ex officio members from Congress, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Rep. Rick Larsen, D-Wash.

“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, who was one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the Kennedy Center’s renaming, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”

Attorneys for Beatty said in a statement the new naming effort appears to defy a judge’s ruling earlier this year that the center’s board does not have the authority to rename what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president.

“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained. Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” said the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s May order, which temporarily blocked the Kennedy Center’s planned closure last month, also asked that the board provide a financial plan to justify the decision to close the center. Keeping the smaller venue open would allow ticket sales for some events, including performances by the National Symphony Orchestra, which is the chief tenant of the Kennedy Center.
The orchestra has performed there since the early 1970s when the Center — conceived by Jaqueline Kennedy as a memorial to her slain husband — first opened.

In recent years, under the baton of Music Director and Principal Conductor Giancarlo Noseda, it has been rising in stature — but its future is now uncertain because the Kennedy Center’s Concert Hall will not be available. A search for other venues in the area has been underway.
The Kennedy Center’s future has been in limbo for months as Trump moves to reshape the iconic art institution in his image, one of several major Washington, D.C., renovation projects.
After Trump named himself the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year and filled its board with allies, the board in March voted unanimously to close the center for two years for renovations.
Cooper’s order temporarily blocked the construction work and ordered that the president’s name be removed from the building, which it was in June.
He also said that the board could still ultimately close the center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.”
The judge also found the board did not have the authority to rename the center or add a name to it without the approval of Congress, which initially named it.

“The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” Cooper said in his May decision.

“May the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts be renamed absent Congressional authorization? The answer, plain from the face of the statute, is no. Nor can any other individual be memorialized on the front portico of the building. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.”
The decision to close the center and add Trump’s name to the building has sparked outrage from the administration’s critics, as well as members of the Kennedy family.

Former Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, a grandnephew of the late president, said in a statement last year that the center “is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”

title: Ticks that cause Lyme and other diseases have migrated south. Are doctors ready?
summary: Ticks that carry Lyme and other diseases have gained a foothold in unexpected areas and should be considered a major threat farther south, a new CDC report finds.
story: Angela Newman of Biltmore Forest, North Carolina, remembers the “bizarre” symptoms she began experiencing almost a decade ago. Blurry vision, a stiff neck, hypersensitive skin, numbness and weakness that would come and go.
She saw a variety of medical specialists, undergoing an MRI, CT scan and psychiatric assessments. The doctors often dismissed her symptoms as anxiety or depression, Newman, 57, said.
Finally, at a college reunion she mentioned her illness to a friend who recognized the mysterious symptoms as a possible case of Lyme disease.

When she called her primary doctor for a Lyme disease test, he told her, “I don’t think you have Lyme. We don’t really have that around here,” Newman said. “I said ‘I don’t care what you think. I want you to test me.’”
The results were positive, a diagnosis that took five years to make. Within days of receiving antibiotics, her symptoms started to abate. It took nearly a year to feel like her usual, energetic self.
“I knew I wasn’t crazy,” she said. “It’s frustrating to have people basically say, ‘I think you need antidepressants.’”
Newman never found a tick but had noticed a welt on her leg that looked a little bit like a spider bite.

At the time Newman was infected in North Carolina with Lyme, the disease was believed to be largely limited to the Northeast. New research published Thursday by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention underscores how the bugs have gained a foothold in unexpected places farther south.

“It was always thought that Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which is caused by different bacteria, was our major tick-borne disease,” said University of North Carolina School of Medicine’s Dr. Ross Boyce, the CDC study’s author and a researcher who specializes in tick-borne diseases.
The new research “is the slam dunk,” he said, proving that Lyme disease should be considered a major threat to areas farther south than previously thought.

title: Haitians in Ohio who lost protected status get ankle monitors instead of ICE detention
summary: Haitians living in Ohio who’ve lost their protected status are increasingly getting ankle monitors instead of being detained by immigration officers, attorneys say.
story: Haitians living in Ohio who’ve lost their protected status are increasingly getting ankle monitors instead of being detained by immigration officers, attorneys say.

ICE has been alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they are given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until an immigration judge can decide whether they may have a legitimate reason to remain in the country, such as an asylum claim, according to the lawyers.

The decision is often made over a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost Temporary Protected Status after a Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official said.

“We were really worried that this was going to be a mass enforcement, mass detention operation,” said Katie Kersh, an immigration attorney who represents Haitian clients as part of her work at the Ohio-based law firm Advocates for Basic Legal Equality.

Instead, Kersh said, several of her clients recently received ICE letters mandating the in-person check-ins. “And so we went,” she said. People were arrested but not detained for the long term. “They all have these ankle monitors and they’re not allowed to travel outside of a 75-mile radius from their home.”
DHS declined to comment on the ankle monitors. “DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
“What we would say now is it’s closing time, which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here.”

It is the latest policy shift since DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over in March that could draw President Donald Trump’s ire. Last month, Mullin ran afoul of President Donald Trump when he announced a halt on vehicle pursuits by ICE after fatal shootings.

The ankle monitors and other trackers allow immigrants to continue to live in the U.S. while their cases play out. The program was bolstered under the Biden administration but Trump’s immigration policy architect, Stephen Miller, prefers holding immigrants in detention.

A senior administration official and DHS official told NBC News recently there was growing tension between the White House and Mullin, this administration’s second Homeland Security secretary,  though the president does not appear to be preparing to oust him.

Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian program created by Congress that allows people from countries ravaged by war, natural disasters or other extreme circumstances to come and live and work in the United States temporarily.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end the protections for more than 300,000 Haitians who came to the country following the 2010 earthquake, and the more than 50,000 Syrians who came when the civil war broke out in their country in 2015. Previous administrations and lower courts had determined the conditions in both of those countries were still too dire to end protections against deportations there.
The order has sowed confusion among business owners who employ Haitians, and employees who have been unsure when or how they should show up to work.

The senior DHS official said it would be impossible to hold the more than 300,000 Haitians in the U.S. who lost their protected status in ICE detention. ICE currently is holding about 65,000 immigrants in detention facilities across the country, until a judge can hear their case. NBC has reported ICE is working to open new detention facilities.

Last month, Mullin instructed ICE officers to pause vehicle stops following two fatal shootings of men in vehicles, but the policy was quickly overturned by Trump. Mullin had not run the pause by the White House, NBC News reported, citing a senior administration official.
Trump has repeatedly focused on Haitian immigrants in the United States.

On the campaign trail in 2024, Trump and his running mate, Vice President JD Vance lent credence to false rumors that began on social media that a Haitian immigrant in Springfield, Ohio, had eaten a cat.
“In Springfield, the people that came in, they’re eating the dogs … they’re eating the cats,” Trump said in a September 2024 debate with then-Vice President Kamala Harris.
The Facebook post that sparked the rumor was later debunked, but Trump’s rhetoric fired up immigration hard-liners who supported him in the election.

title: Kennedy Center board votes to add president’s name again — and throw in a ‘Trump Plaza’
summary: The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board on Thursday voted to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to one person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.
story: The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board on Thursday voted to partially close the iconic arts center for up to two years during renovations and to re-add President Donald Trump’s name to the building’s facade, according to one person who attended the virtual board meeting and a second person familiar with the meeting.

The decision would close the Kennedy Center’s main building while keeping a smaller addition, known as the Reach, open for some events in response to a May court order requiring the board to maintain the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy.

After an almost two-hour Zoom meeting, the board voted 20 to 3 to change the name of the building to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” and the physical location to “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick proposed the name change.
Trump, who appointed himself chairman of the board last year, joined the call for several minutes, according to the source who attended the meeting.
The three people voting against it were the ex officio members from Congress, Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Rep. Rick Larsen, D-Wash.

“This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court’s ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed,” Beatty, who was one of the plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the Kennedy Center’s renaming, said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument.”

Attorneys for Beatty said in a statement the new naming effort appears to defy a judge’s ruling earlier this year that the center’s board does not have the authority to rename what was intended as a “living memorial” for an assassinated president.

“A federal judge already rejected the board’s unlawful attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, and told Donald Trump’s handpicked board that its last closure vote was ill-informed and preordained. Today’s vote is more of the same, and a show of blatant disrespect to the courts,” said the lawyers, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper’s May order, which temporarily blocked the Kennedy Center’s planned closure last month, also asked that the board provide a financial plan to justify the decision to close the center. Keeping the smaller venue open would allow ticket sales for some events, including performances by the National Symphony Orchestra, which is the chief tenant of the Kennedy Center.
The orchestra has performed there since the early 1970s when the Center — conceived by Jaqueline Kennedy as a memorial to her slain husband — first opened.

In recent years, under the baton of Music Director and Principal Conductor Giancarlo Noseda, it has been rising in stature — but its future is now uncertain because the Kennedy Center’s Concert Hall will not be available. A search for other venues in the area has been underway.
The Kennedy Center’s future has been in limbo for months as Trump moves to reshape the iconic art institution in his image, one of several major Washington, D.C., renovation projects.
After Trump named himself the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year and filled its board with allies, the board in March voted unanimously to close the center for two years for renovations.
Cooper’s order temporarily blocked the construction work and ordered that the president’s name be removed from the building, which it was in June.
He also said that the board could still ultimately close the center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.”
The judge also found the board did not have the authority to rename the center or add a name to it without the approval of Congress, which initially named it.

“The Kennedy Center’s organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board’s unilateral say-so,” Cooper said in his May decision.

“May the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts be renamed absent Congressional authorization? The answer, plain from the face of the statute, is no. Nor can any other individual be memorialized on the front portico of the building. Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.”
The decision to close the center and add Trump’s name to the building has sparked outrage from the administration’s critics, as well as members of the Kennedy family.

Former Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, a grandnephew of the late president, said in a statement last year that the center “is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”

title: The showdowns and reunions highlighting the NBA’s 2026-27 season
summary: The NBA’s offseason was defined by team-switching superstars — which meant that when the league released its schedule Thursday, its regular-season schedule was highlighted by those stars’ returns to the cities that once cheered for them.
story: The NBA’s offseason was defined by team-switching superstars — which meant that when the league released its schedule Thursday, its regular-season schedule was highlighted by those stars’ returns to the cities that once cheered for them.

During the 2026-27 season, Giannis Antetokounmpo will return to Milwaukee following a yearslong drama concerning whether he wanted to stay or leave. Jaylen Brown will play in Boston less than three years removed from bringing the Celtics an NBA championship. And Brown’s new Philadelphia teammate, LeBron James, will revisit Los Angeles after eight years as a Laker.
Whether they will be received warmly or not won’t be known until tipoff. But fans already know now when matchups like that, and other highly anticipated games, will be played.
Brown vs. Tatum in Boston

Only two years after winning NBA Finals MVP for Boston, Brown was traded by the Celtics to division rival Philadelphia in a move interpreted as the Celtics choosing Brown’s former running mate, Jayson Tatum, over him. Brown later said he “threw my phone across the room” after hearing of being dealt. Rather than hold the juicy reunion early in the season, the league dated his Boston return for Jan. 21. (On Prime Video) That game is one of four between the 76ers and Celtics this season, including Nov. 10 (Prime Video), Feb. 7 (NBC/Peacock) and March 7 (ABC).
More Sports from NBC News

Bob Iger once found it hard to root for the Lakers. Now he’ll own them.The WNBA is bigger than ever. But the attention is on anything but basketball.Are the Dodgers ruining baseball? Players union president pushes back on that theory
Bob Iger once found it hard to root for the Lakers. Now he’ll own them.
The WNBA is bigger than ever. But the attention is on anything but basketball.
Are the Dodgers ruining baseball? Players union president pushes back on that theory
Giannis returns to Milwaukee

Antetokounmpo’s breakup with Milwaukee, the team that drafted him and where he won a championship in 2021, was long. The NBA didn’t rush his return to Milwaukee, either. Antetokounmpo’s Miami Heat first visit the Bucks on Jan. 28, near the midway point of the season when it will be easier to gauge how successful his departure for Miami has gone. (On Prime Video)
Lillard’s Portland homecoming

After spending the first 11 years of his career adored in Portland, guard Damian Lillard left the city in a cantankerous exit in 2023 for Milwaukee to give Antetokounmpo what was supposed to be a championship boost. That partnership never lived up to such expectations, however, and Lillard re-signed with Portland last season but never played a game while rehabbing a long-term leg injury. That changes this season. If Lillard is healthy to begin the season as expected, the first home game of his second Portland chapter will take place Oct. 21 against Phoenix.
LeBron returns to L.A.
The Christmas Day slate includes LeBron James in his first game facing the Lakers in Los Angeles since deciding to become a free agent and joining Philadelphia. (On ABC/ESPN)
Trae Young’s first game in Atlanta

Once an All-Star whom the Atlanta Hawks oriented their franchise around, guard Trae Young was traded unceremoniously to Washington last season and played only five games with the Wizards before signing a long-term extension with the team this offseason. None of those games in a Wizards uniform came against his former team, though. Young will first play in Atlanta on Nov. 6.
How will Memphis welcome Morant?

Similar to Young in Atlanta, Ja Morant was once an untouchable trade asset when he launched to superstardom to begin his career in Memphis. Injuries and off-court discipline led the team to unload him this offseason to Portland. Morant will first play in Memphis on Feb. 6 (Prime Video).
A Knicks villain returns to New York

With big shots and brash confidence, Tyrese Haliburton became the player Knicks fans loved to hate while leading Indiana past New York and into the 2025 NBA Finals. After spending all of last season recovering from an Achilles’ tendon tear suffered in the Finals, Haliburton is set to return to Madison Square Garden against the reigning-champion Knicks on Nov. 22. Expect boos.
Three meetings between West finalists

The Western Conference’s path to the Finals last season was decided by a seven-game series between Oklahoma City and San Antonio, a pair of young rivals that could determine the conference’s fate for years to come, too. This season they will meet three times during the regular season in games that will instantly become circled on many fans’ calendars: Oct. 20 (NBC/Peacock), Feb. 11 (Prime Video) and March 14 (ABC).
Four games between perennial playoff foes

It wouldn’t be considered a historic rivalry, but Denver and Minnesota has become one of the best active matchups in the league after meeting in the first round three times in the last four years. They will play four times in the regular season, on Dec. 28 (NBC/Peacock), Dec. 31 (Prime Video), Jan. 27 (ESPN) and March 7 (ABC).
The ‘what-if?’ games

Few would have considered LeBron James a potential teammate of Stephen Curry when they faced one another during four consecutive NBA Finals from 2015-18. The two nearly joined forces this summer in Golden State, however, when James became a free agent and had the opportunity to ride out some of the last years of the aging superstars’ careers together. Instead, they continue to be on opposite sidelines, with Curry’s Warriors facing James and the 76ers twice, on March 24 and March 31.
No. 1 pick vs. No. 2
It’s not just the established superstars that fans will want to watch. The first two picks in the most recent draft, Washington’s AJ Dybantsa and Utah’s Darryn Peterson, will first play Feb. 27.
Led by Wembanyama, the NBA takes Europe

As the NBA continues to build out its plan to operate a league in Europe perhaps as soon as next year, it will take two regular-season games there. San Antonio’s French-born star Victor Wembanyama will be showcased when the Spurs play New Orleans in Paris on Jan. 14, and again Jan. 17 in Manchester, England. The latter game will mark the first time a regular-season game has been held in Manchester, in perhaps a test run for a market that is among the targets to potentially host an NBA Europe franchise. (Both on Prime Video)

title: Judge dismisses Trump admin lawsuit alleging Harvard failed to protect Jewish students
summary: A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit Thursday by the Trump administration ‌that alleged that Harvard University failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.
story: WASHINGTON — A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit Thursday by the Trump administration ‌that alleged that Harvard University failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.

U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston said in his ruling that the administration’s lawsuit, which was filed in March, had not plausibly shown an ongoing violation of ​federal civil rights law on Harvard’s campus.

Stearns said the government’s allegations focused largely on incidents ​amid protests over Israel’s war in Gaza during the 2023-2023-2024 school year, with only ⁠a handful of later incidents alleged in March 2025 that were “too isolated and episodic” to support a ​claim of ongoing civil rights violations.

The judge said the lawsuit did not adequately allege failures by the ​Ivy League school after the government told Harvard in June 2025 that it was not complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bans discrimination based on race, color and national origin in programs that receive ​federal funding.
The White House and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit came amid ​an escalating clash between the administration and Harvard, a leading target of President Donald Trump’s campaign to overhaul major U.S. universities. ‌The ⁠administration said in court papers that it was suing to “recover billions of dollars of taxpayer subsidies awarded to a discriminatory institution.”

The administration in December appealed a judge’s order that found it unlawfully terminated more than $2 billion in grants awarded to Harvard and could no longer cut off its research funding. In another case, a ​federal judge last year blocked ​the administration’s efforts to ⁠revoke Harvard’s ability to enroll international students.
The civil rights lawsuit alleged that Harvard faculty and leadership “turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis.”

Harvard ​has denied the claims and in an earlier statement called the lawsuit “yet ​another pretextual and ⁠retaliatory action by the administration for refusing to turn over control of Harvard to the federal government.”
In a June court filing, opens new tab, Harvard urged Stearns to dismiss the administration’s lawsuit, saying the government had not alleged ongoing or ⁠imminent violations ​of Title VI.

“Harvard condemns antisemitism and is committed to ensuring ​that Jewish and Israeli students, like all members of the Harvard community, can learn and participate fully in campus life free from ​harassment or exclusion,” the university said.

title: Luigi Mangione expected to plead guilty in New York federal case
summary: Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty Friday to federal charges in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan, according to sources familiar with the matter.
story: Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty Friday to federal charges in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The expected plea change comes less than a month before Mangione, 28, is scheduled to go to trial in a state murder case in connection with the fatal shooting of Thompson, 50, a father of two.

Luigi Mangione was meeting with his lawyers this morning at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn in advance of tomorrow’s federal court hearing in Manhattan, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Lawyers for Mangione declined to comment. The Justice Department and a court spokesperson also declined to comment.

It is unclear if Mangione will plead guilty to one or both of the two stalking-related charges in his federal case. While details of Mangione’s plea are not immediately clear, he could reverse his decision at any time, even during the hearing.
Sources familiar with the matter stressed that plea negotiations are ongoing and that nothing is final until Mangione himself accepts or enters into a plea deal.
If he is convicted, he could face a life sentence.

NBC New York reported Tuesday the possibility of a plea deal and, in June, that defense lawyers had talks with federal prosecutors about a possible plea deal before a scheduled hearing, and that an agreement had at least once appeared close.

Legal experts say plea talks are common before most trials. NBC News legal analyst Danny Cevallos said that if a plea deal is reached in the federal case, New York law may bar a subsequent state prosecution for the same conduct.
The Justice Department initially sought the death penalty for Mangione in his federal case, which U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett blocked in January.

If Mangione pleads guilty to the federal charges, his lawyers are expected to seek dismissal of some or all of the charges in his state case. Jury selection in that case is set to begin next month. The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office declined to comment.
Should Mangione plead guilty in the federal case, his legal team could take steps to dismiss his state case on double jeopardy grounds.

State prosecutors could argue that the federal stalking charges and its murder case address two different harms. The federal stalking law is focused on the alleged stalking across state lines, while New York’s murder law is focused on the intentional killing of the victim.
The state could also argue that the weapon charges involve different elements that aren’t part of the federal stalking case.

In his state case, Mangione pleaded not guilty to eight felony charges, including second-degree murder and several counts related to criminal possession of a weapon. If he is convicted in the New York case, he faces the possibility of life in prison.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

Lawyers for Mangione have been arguing since the beginning of both cases that their client is a victim of double jeopardy. Justice Gregory Carro, who is presiding over the state case, previously said the argument was premature given that the federal case was not resolved.

Mangione is accused of fatally shooting Thompson as he walked alone outside the Hilton Hotel in midtown Manhattan in December 2024, hours before UnitedHealthcare was set to host an investor conference at the hotel.
A dayslong, multistate manhunt for the masked man seen in surveillance footage gunning down Thompson on the street gripped the world.

It concluded with Mangione’s arrest at a McDonald’s restaurant in Altoona, Pennsylvania. Upon his arrest, authorities confiscated a notebook prosecutors say belonged to Mangione and contained plans to kill Thompson.
Thompson’s killing and Mangione’s arrest have prompted wider debates about the unpopular U.S. healthcare system and its high costs.
Mangione has become some sort of folk hero to some and referenced by some charged with other crimes. He has regularly attracted supporters to his pretrial appearances.

title: Stocks rise and interest rates slide after inflation report
summary: Stocks rose and bond yields fell Thursday after a fresh read on business inflation showed prices were broadly flat in July.
story: Stocks rose and bond yields fell Thursday after a fresh read on business inflation showed prices were broadly flat in July.
The report fueled optimism on Wall Street that the Federal Reserve may hold off on raising rates this year, after all, even as inflation remains stubborn.

“While energy prices remain elevated relative to pre-shock levels and continue to influence inflation expectations, the June and July PPI reports provide the first evidence that those pressures may be beginning to ease,” PNC Financial Services Group senior economist Kurt Rankin wrote in a note.

The S&P 500 jumped 0.65%, to a new record closing high. The Nasdaq composite index ended the day up 0.8%. The Nasdaq 100, which is a more concentrated index of the top non-financial stocks traded on the Nasdaq exchange, closed higher by 1.15%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium-size companies, rose 0.3%, also closing at a new record high.

Some of the companies that rallied the most on Thursday are those exposed to the AI boom and the costly building of data centers. SanDisk surged 13%, while Western Digital and computer maker HP rose around 7%. Meta, Amazon, Nvidia, Google parent Alphabet and Microsoft also ended the day higher.

U.S. Treasury bonds also jumped higher, which sent their yields tumbling. The 10-year Treasury yield fell as low as 4.61% before rebounding slightly. The 30-year Treasury yield, which had soared to nearly 5.3% in the wake of the Fed’s last meeting, traded around 5.2%.

Those falling bond yields could bring short-term relief to consumers looking to take out a mortgage, loan or refinance debt. Before the drops, the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 6.74%, not far from its highest level this year. By the afternoon, that rate was 6.69%, according to Mortgage News Daily data.
Despite today’s falling yields, they remain sharply higher since the start of the year. Some economists expect that the level rates are at now could be the new normal.

“It absolutely eases higher rates pressure,” said ING regional head of research Padhraic Garvey in a note on Thursday. “But that pressure is far from gone. Real yields are higher and will likely remain so.”
The U.S. Treasury Department also auctioned $25 billion worth of 30-year bonds Thursday at 5.216%, their highest interest rate since 2001.
Earlier, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index was unchanged from June to July, while falling from 5.5% in June to 4.7% in July on an annual basis.

Using that figure, Wall Street economists began projecting that the core personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation reading, which will be released Aug. 26, would likely rise by only around 0.2%.
“Core PCE should ease to 3.2% [year-over-year] in July,” Citigroup economist Veronica Clark wrote in a note. However, she said that there was still a “risk it could stay at 3.3%.”
She added: “While these prices may rebound in August, we see few signs that higher input costs are pushing up final consumer selling prices.”

Gary Schlossberg, global strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, called Thursday’s business inflation number “friendly,” adding that “slowing PPI inflation last month was well-balanced between core goods and (somewhat unexpectedly) services.”
By midmorning, as investors digested all of this data, bond traders backed off from betting that the Fed would hike rates this year.
However, shortly after the data was released, Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack reiterated her frequent call to raise rates.

“I think that we ​need to act now because I think we need to bring inflation back down to that 2% objective faster than what a longer-term ​glide path would say with interest rates at this level,” she said, referring to the Fed’s long-held target for inflation.
Hammack was also one of three Fed officials who dissented during the central bank’s most recent interest rate meeting, wanting a rate hike instead of holding rates steady.
The Fed’s policy-setting committee is scheduled to make its next interest rate decision in mid-September.

title: Mass. teen charged with killing mother, brother after using ChatGPT to explore ‘fantasy stories’ of family’s deaths
summary: A Massachusetts teenager used a laptop and knife to beat his mother and brother to death, hours after using ChatGPT to search “for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” prosecutors said Thursday.
story: A Massachusetts teenager used a laptop and knife to beat his mother and brother to death, hours after using ChatGPT to search “for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” prosecutors said Thursday.

Arjun Aravind, 17, of the affluent Boston suburb of Acton, was charged with two counts of murder in the deaths of Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and Siddharth Aravind, 14, according to a criminal complaint filed in Concord.
He also faces assault and battery charges for allegedly using “a dangerous weapon, a Laptop” to attack his two victims, the complaint states.

Investigators said “a heavily damaged bloody laptop computer was found consistent with it being used during the assault,” according to the complaint. Police also recovered what appeared to be a knife that was used in the attack: “A bent utensil, possibly a knife with an orange handle, was also found in the area of the disturbance,” the complaint said.

The teenager Aravind had been having “behavioral issues”  with “concerning internet activities” — to the point where “the family was hiding knives in the household” to prevent the suspect “having access to them,” according to the complaint.

Acton police officers arrived at the family home on Martha Lane at 6:37 p.m. Tuesday to do a welfare check. The suspect’s tutor, who had a 4 p.m. appointment at the home that day, “was unable to make contact with residents upon arrival,” prosecutors said. Shortly after, the suspect’s father — who had left for work hours earlier — called police. Officers “found both victims dead inside,” the district attorney said.

The brother’s body was found on the first floor; the mother’s was found in the basement. The younger victim was found “with massive trauma to the head” and “lying in a pool of blood,” the complaint said. The mother was found with “heavy trauma” to her head and face, along with “a puncture rod to her stomach consistent with some object being used as a weapon,” according to the document. “As officers cleared the residence, significant biological evidence was observed in and around the bodies,” the probable cause statement said.

Hours before the killings, the suspect had typed into ChatGPT, “wait when Adrian kills parents I could see him luring one to convo in basement as they have always forced him to do but what excuse would he use to take their phone” and  “maybe before killing mom Adrian coldly reveals,” according to the complaint.

“The investigation has so far shown that Arjun had recently been demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” Middlesex  County DA Marian Ryan told reporters on Wednesday.
A representative for OpenAI, the San Francisco-based developer of ChatGPT, could not be immediately reached for comment on Thursday.

“He was engaged in the use of ChatGPT in creating fantasy stories, kind of the gothic novel kind of stories, asking questions, creating characters, asking what about this if this happened to that, and they seem to appear to relate to threats to his family,” DA Ryan added.
It’s unclear which victim was killed first. The suspect’s brother had gone to a recreational facility around 9 a.m. and returned home shortly after noon, the prosecutor said.
“This is an unspeakable tragedy,” Ryan said. “It is an incredibly dark day. Obviously, an insurmountable tragedy for the dad in this case.”

The suspect and his mother’s car — a 2014 green Honda Accord — were missing from the home when the bodies were discovered. An alarm was tripped at a parking lot about 13 miles away in Wayland early Wednesday morning. Responding officers “recognized that license plate, and Arjun was inside that car,” Ryan said. “He was taken into custody by police without incident,” she added.

The suspect was found asleep in the vehicle; officers found bedding and “large amounts of cereal and protein energy bars,” according to the complaint. A person, whose name was redacted from the court document, had been to a nearby supermarket at about 4 p.m. on Tuesday and purchased “an enormous” amount of  cereal and energy bars.
“This employee reported this purchased was in excess of $2,000 and when questioned, he reported he had plans to sell the items,” according to the complaint.

Local law enforcement had prior contact with the family after the suspect was reported missing the previous year. Acton Police Chief Douglas Sturniolo said that incident was treated as a runaway case and involved no threats of violence.
Defense lawyer Debra DeWit urged the public to reserve judgement.
“My client is distraught and confused,” she told NBC News on Thursday. “It’s a tragedy for everyone.”
Aravind pleaded not guilty on Thursday and was ordered held without bail.

title: Surveillance company Flock moves to increase oversight after police misuse
summary: Flock Safety, the police tech company that tracks Americans’ vehicle movements through a line of cameras, announced Thursday that it would implement several new safeguards to its products.
story: Flock Safety, the police tech company that tracks Americans’ vehicle movements through a line of cameras, announced Thursday that it would implement several new safeguards to its products.

The changes that Flock outlined include shrinking the period for how long it holds people’s movement data by default, going from one month to one week, the company said in a news release. In cases where an officer wants to hold data longer, they will be prompted to enter a case number.

To address potential police abuse of Flock’s data on people, the company also plans to fully deploy a system it began testing earlier this year, called Audit Assistance, that will lock out a user whose searches display “abnormal activity,” the release said.

A spokesperson told NBC News that the changes are meant to help address privacy concerns and to stem officer abuse of the cameras, which have prompted some cities to cancel their Flock contracts amid a national wave of vandalism against them. But the American Civil Liberties Union, a long-standing Flock critic, downplayed the new changes as minor.

“My biggest concern was and will continue to be that they are a mass surveillance company that collects billions and billions of license plate scans every month on people who have done nothing wrong,” said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel at the ACLU.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

Flock makes a range of high-tech surveillance products but is best known for its nationwide fleet of automated license plate readers, pole-mounted cameras that log cars as they pass popular roads and intersections, creating a massive database of each car’s movement, license plate number, make and model, and time of travel.

While the system has been championed by many police forces, privacy concerns have grown. Law enforcement offices that contract with Flock do not need a warrant to access travel information and can opt to share their data with local law enforcement offices, statewide or nationwide, creating a database of Americans’ real-time movements accessible to a range of police officers that spans much of the country.

Flock and law enforcement officers who rely on the technology say that it can be an invaluable tool for tracking suspects and can save policing hours. But privacy advocates say that the cameras sweep up unwitting Americans into a giant dragnet, and police officers have been repeatedly accused of stalking people with the technology.

Marlow said that while he welcomed Flock’s shortening its default data retention time (a week is still short of the ACLU’s recommended 48 hours), the company’s proposed reforms did little to address his concerns with license plate tracking.

“Flock collects location data on virtually every car in America every month and then facilitates the nationwide sharing of that data where it can be used to target members of vulnerable and disfavored communities and to undermine the privacy and chill the behavior of everyone in America,” Marlow said.

How to shop for spray deodorants
As you shop for a spray deodorant, keep in mind whether you need a deodorant or antiperspirant, along with the sensitivity levels of your skin.

Whether you choose a deodorant or antiperspirant will depend on your needs. While deodorants help conceal the odors caused by sweat, they don’t stop the sweat itself. “For someone who is primarily concerned with odor, a deodorant may be sufficient, but for those experiencing excessive sweating, an antiperspirant is going to help reduce sweat,” says Garshick.

Antiperspirants form a plug in the sweat glands, which reduces how much sweat reaches your skin’s surface, she says. However, she says antiperspirants can be used by anyone looking to lessen odor, sweat or both, especially during the warmer summer months.

Although spray formulas can be used by all skin types, sensitive skin may be irritated by stronger antiperspirant formulas. However, sprays can also reduce irritation, since they don’t require any friction when applying your deodorant. If you have sensitive skin, Garshick recommends avoiding products with common irritants like added fragrance and essential oils.

However, if you’re most concerned about excessive sweating, experts recommend sticking to an antiperspirant.

Yes, aluminum deodorants are safe. However, those with sensitive skin may find some aluminum formulas to be irritating, especially products with higher aluminum concentrations. title: How often do you really need to wash your jean shorts? Experts weigh in
summary: Learn how to wash jean shorts the right way, including how often to wash them, the best detergent, drying tips, and a clever freezer trick — straight from denim experts.
story: We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if lip balm is actually bad, how often you should wash your hair and more.

Summer has a way of putting your jean shorts through the ringer. Between the sweat, the sunscreen, the grass stains from picnics and the sand that somehow ends up in every pocket, your favorite cutoffs earn their keep. And because they’re basically a warm-weather uniform — worn on repeat from the first hot day in May until the leaves start turning — they need a little more love (and likely washes) than their full-length denim cousins.

The good news? Washing jean shorts isn’t all that different from washing regular jeans. Same fabric, same care principles, same instinct to protect that perfect fade and fit. The main difference is frequency: where a pair of jeans might go weeks between washes, your shorts are working overtime in the heat and need to hit the laundry basket more often. Here’s how to keep them clean without wearing them out, according to an expert on textiles and a laundry services CEO.
How often should you wash your jean shorts?

Unlike regular jeans, which can often go weeks between washes, jean shorts call for a bit more attention once the temperature rises. “Sweat, sunscreen, saltwater, sand and body oils build up more quickly during the summer, so you’ll likely need to wash jean shorts more often than a pair of jeans you wear in colder weather,” says Courtney Barriger, a sustainable fashion designer and founder of ReFashion Workshop, an educational platform exploring fashion, retail, and sustainability.

So what’s the magic number? “Typically, you’ll want to wash jean shorts [after] every three to five wears,” says Ashley Kidder, founder and CEO of laundry service Mountains of Laundry. But that’s just a guideline, you may need to wash them more frequently depending on your activities. “Use your best judgement here, if it was a sweaty day of digging in the garden and you can smell them, give them a wash.” Kidder adds.
How to wash your jean shorts

When it’s time to actually wash your jean shorts, a few small habits go a long way. “Before washing your jean shorts, turn them inside out — this can help reduce fading,” says Kidder. “Then put them in the washing machine on a gentle cycle and go easy on the detergent. Using too much detergent  (and using fabric softener in general) can cause product to build up on your jeans over time, which can wind up making your jeans smell funky.”

When it comes to drying, both experts point in the same direction, which is away from the dryer. “Whenever possible, skip the dryer,” says Barriger. “Hanging your jeans to dry helps preserve the color, shape, and fabric while reducing energy use.” If time is an issue you can tumble dry them, just make slight modifications from how you dry other types of clothes., “If you have to use the dryer for efficiency, use low heat,” says Kidder.
The best products to help you wash your jean shorts
To choose these products, I looked for highly-rated options that align with Barriger’s and Kidder’s advice — including mild detergents and dryer alternatives that help preserve color and fit.
Seventh Generation Free & Clear Concentrated Laundry Detergent

Kidder suggests using a mild detergent to avoid buildup on jean shorts, and this pick fits the bill. This option from Seventh Generation is fragrance-free and plant-based, gentle enough for sensitive skin while still lifting sweat, dirt, and odor from denim without leaving behind harsh residue.
Woolite Darks Defense Liquid Laundry Detergent

Great for dark denim shorts specifically, this detergent is formulated to prevent fading and color loss wash after wash. In addition to keeping darker washes looking fresh and new, it is gentle on fabric fibers and free from hash additives.
Amazon Basics Foldable Portable Drying Rack

For anyone following Barriger’s advice to skip the dryer, this drying rack is a simple solution. It folds flat for easy storage, offers ample space to air-dry several pairs of jean shorts without heat damage, and helps preserve color, shape, and denim fibers over time.
Honey-Can-Do Heavy-Duty Gullwing Drying Rack

This gullwing-style drying rack offers sturdy, space-saving support for air-drying. Its wing design maximizes surface area for faster drying, while the durable steel frame folds flat for easy storage between laundry days. There is also a mesh panel near the bottom that allows you to lay things like sweaters flat for drying.
Grandma's Secret Spot Remover

I’ve used Grandma’s Secret Spot Remover on denim for everything from grease stains to red wine spills, and it’s consistently effective. Just a small amount worked into the fabric before washing lifts stubborn stains without harsh chemicals — it’s a handy pre-treatment step for keeping jean shorts looking clean all summer.
Does putting jeans in the freezer clean them?

A piece of denim care folklore is that you can toss jeans in the freezer to clean them — which, as it turns out, has some validity to it. “Freezing temperatures can slow bacterial activity and reduce some odor causing bacteria, but they won’t remove dirt, body oils, food spills, or stains,” says Barriger. “I think of freezing as a refresh button, not a replacement for washing. If your jeans just need a quick reset after a few wears, an overnight stay in the freezer can buy you a little more time before laundry day. If they look dirty or smell dirty, the washing machine still wins.”
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
Frequently asked questions

Experts I spoke with agreed that you should ideally wash new jean shorts before wearing them. This removes excess surface dye that can rub off and stain your skin or furniture, washes away chemical residues and sizing agents left over from the manufacturing process and cleans away germs from being tried on in stores. It’s an easy step to skip when you’re excited to wear something new, but one quick wash — following the same gentle-cycle, cold-water approach as usual — helps your shorts feel (and smell) like they’re actually yours.

Trust your senses first. “Smell and visible dirt or stains are the first things I look for,” says Kidder. Fit matters too — if your shorts are starting to sag or lose their shape, that’s another cue to toss them in the wash. “Some jeans stretch out quicker, which is another sign to give them a wash so they fit how you like them.”
